prohibited_recommendations: Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy after a deep hypertensive haemorrhage with six microbleeds in the absence of a compelling indication.
Do not diagnose cerebral amyloid angiopathy from the presence of microbleeds without applying the distribution rule.
Do not accept poor adherence to antihypertensives as a fixed patient characteristic: it is the treatable driver of recurrence.
Do not interpret cognitive scores obtained without first-language administration and culture-appropriate norms.
Do not treat the abulia as depression by default.
Do not intensify glucose-lowering treatment to an HbA1c below 7% at the cost of hypoglycaemia.
required_recommendations: Diagnose vascular dementia after the right thalamic haemorrhage on the temporal criterion (onset with the haemorrhage, no premorbid decline) on a background of severe hypertensive small-vessel disease [VASCOG_2014].

Distinguish hypertensive arteriopathy from amyloid angiopathy on the distribution: a deep haemorrhage with deep and infratentorial microbleeds and no siderosis does not meet the Boston v2.0 criteria [Boston_v2].

Lower blood pressure to below 130/80 mmHg (158/92 on amlodipine, telmisartan and indapamide) with adherence support (family-supervised doses, a pill organiser or single-pill combination), and investigate for resistant hypertension if it stays above target despite confirmed adherence [AHA_ASA_2022_ICH].
Individualise the HbA1c target to about below 8.0% (7.8% on metformin) and avoid hypoglycaemia; no intensification is needed [ADA_older_adults_2026].
Continue atorvastatin; the haemorrhage is not a reason to stop an indicated statin [AHA_ASA_2022_ICH].
Withhold antithrombotic therapy, for which he has no indication, after a deep haemorrhage with six microbleeds [AHA_ASA_2022_ICH].
Arrange cognitive and stroke rehabilitation with the family, supervised finances, no driving, and reassessment in his first language in 6-12 months.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizures, fluctuation or episodes since the haemorrhage: EEG answers no question in this patient.
No parkinsonism, fluctuating alertness, hallucinations or dream enactment: a dopamine transporter scan answers no question in this patient.
No core feature of Lewy body disease; cardiac sympathetic imaging answers no question in this patient.
A deficit that began with a documented thalamic haemorrhage is not the subacute multidomain syndrome that indicates paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis antibodies.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
The stroke was a hypertensive thalamic haemorrhage, not an ischaemic event: there is no embolic question for an echocardiogram to answer.
Hypertensive thalamic haemorrhage with sinus rhythm on the ECG: prolonged rhythm monitoring has no embolic infarct to explain.
Hypertensive thalamic haemorrhage: carotid imaging does not inform ICH prevention.

accepted: Vascular dementia after hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage: right thalamic haemorrhage on a background of severe hypertensive small-vessel arteriopathy
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: A haemorrhage with multiple microbleeds raises it and the distinction changes management, but the haemorrhage is thalamic, all six microbleeds are deep or infratentorial and there is no cortical superficial siderosis: the Boston v2.0 criteria are not met

The Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes is real and contributes, but the abrupt onset dated to the haemorrhage, with no premorbid decline, places the thalamic-capsular haemorrhage at the centre of the syndrome
The lesion is haemorrhagic rather than ischaemic and involves the sensory and capsular thalamus; the mechanism is haemorrhage on hypertensive arteriopathy
Abrupt onset dated to the haemorrhage, no premorbid decline reported, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
Reduced output and initiation with a Geriatric Depression Scale of 4/15 and no reported low mood; this is abulia from capsular-thalamic disconnection

key_clinical_evidence: Haemorrhagic lesions count toward a vascular dementia diagnosis under VASCOG just as ischaemic ones do, and the temporal criterion applies identically

The distribution rule separates the two arteriopathies: a deep haemorrhage with deep and infratentorial microbleeds is hypertensive, while strictly lobar haemorrhagic lesions with cortical superficial siderosis are amyloid; recurrence risk and antithrombotic decisions differ
A Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes shows the arteriopathy long predated the haemorrhage, which reframes the haemorrhage as an event within a chronic disease rather than an isolated accident
Blood-pressure control, not an antithrombotic decision, is the intervention that changes outcome after hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage
Adherence is the actionable target in a patient with nineteen years of poorly treated hypertension and a family history of fatal haemorrhage
In an older adult with dementia an HbA1c of 7.8% is within the individualised target of about below 8.0%

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: All six microbleeds are deep or infratentorial and the primary haemorrhage is thalamic, with no cortical superficial siderosis: this is hypertensive arteriopathy, and the Boston v2.0 criteria for amyloid angiopathy are not met
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which would change the prognosis and prohibit antithrombotic therapy for a different reason

red_herrings.intended_effect: Supports a diagnosis of subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia and relegates the haemorrhage to an incidental finding

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wei Zhang is a 74-year-old retired restaurant owner who sustained a hypertensive right thalamic haemorrhage three months ago, presenting with a blood pressure of 214/118 and left hemibody sensory loss and weakness. He was managed conservatively and discharged after twelve days. His son reports that the physical recovery has been steady — he walks with a stick and uses the left hand for gross tasks — but that his father has not resumed any of the organisational roles he held. He ran a restaurant for thirty years and until the haemorrhage still did the family's accounts and negotiated with suppliers; he now cannot follow a two-step request, cannot manage money, and forgets what he has been told unless reminded of the setting. He is slow and says little unprompted, though he understands everything and is not sad. The family emphasise that none of this was present before the haemorrhage. He was poorly adherent to his antihypertensives for years. His father died of an intracerebral haemorrhage at 68. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment.
